title: Can an abstract class have a constructor (yes — it runs when a concrete subclass is instantiated via `super()`), and can an interface have a constructor (no — interfaces cannot hold instance state, so there is nothing to initialize)?
shortTitle: Can an abstract class have a constructor, and can an interface have a constructor?

s1_definition.profdef: An abstract class can and often does have a constructor. Although you cannot instantiate an abstract class directly, its constructor runs as part of building a concrete subclass instance, invoked through the subclass's `super(...)` call, and its purpose is to initialize the fields the abstract class declares. An interface cannot have a constructor, because an interface holds no instance state; its fields are implicitly `public static final` constants that are initialized at class-load time, so there is no per-instance data to initialize and therefore nothing for a constructor to do.
s1_definition.analogy: An abstract class is like a partially filled master account template at National Bank of India. You cannot open an account from the template alone, but every real account opened from it reuses the template's setup steps, filling in the shared base details like the opening date and branch code. That shared setup is the abstract class's constructor, running automatically whenever a real account is created. An interface, on the other hand, is like a published code of conduct the bank posts on the wall: it only lists rules every employee must follow and a few fixed notices. It owns no desk, no cash drawer, no personal state, so there is nothing to set up and no setup ceremony, which is why it has no constructor.
s1_definition.oneliner: Abstract classes have constructors that run via a subclass's `super()` to initialize shared state, while interfaces have no constructors because they hold no instance state to initialize.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** An abstract class can and often does have a constructor. Although you cannot instantiate an abstract class directly, its constructor runs as part of building a concrete subclass instance, invoked through the subclass's `super(...)` call, and its purpose is to initialize the fields the abstract class declares. An interface cannot have a constructor, because an interface holds no instance state; its fields are implicitly `public static final` constants that are initialized at class-load time, so there is no per-instance data to initialize and therefore nothing for a constructor to do.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** An abstract class is like a partially filled master account template at National Bank of India. You cannot open an account from the template alone, but every real account opened from it reuses the template's setup steps, filling in the shared base details like the opening date and branch code. That shared setup is the abstract class's constructor, running automatically whenever a real account is created. An interface, on the other hand, is like a published code of conduct the bank posts on the wall: it only lists rules every employee must follow and a few fixed notices. It owns no desk, no cash drawer, no personal state, so there is nothing to set up and no setup ceremony, which is why it has no constructor.

**One line to remember:** Abstract classes have constructors that run via a subclass's `super()` to initialize shared state, while interfaces have no constructors because they hold no instance state to initialize.

sections.s2_technical:
An abstract class is a class you cannot instantiate on its own, but it is still a class, so it participates fully in the construction chain. It can declare instance fields, and those fields need initializing, so it can and should have a constructor. You cannot write `new AbstractThing()`, but when you write `new ConcreteSubclass(...)`, the subclass constructor's `super(...)` call invokes the abstract class's constructor, which runs before the subclass body. For example, an abstract `Account` with an `accountId` field can validate and set it in its constructor, and every concrete account type inherits that guaranteed initialization.

Because the abstract class constructor runs top-down like any superclass constructor, it is the correct place to enforce invariants on the shared state. If the abstract `Account` requires a non-null id and a non-negative balance, placing those checks in its constructor means no subclass can ever skip them, since the subclass must call `super(...)` to reach that constructor. This is a common and powerful design: put the mandatory shared setup in the abstract base's constructor so every concrete type gets it for free and consistently.

An abstract class constructor can also be declared non-public, often `protected`, to signal that only subclasses should invoke it. Writing `protected Account(String id, BigDecimal balance)` documents the intent that this constructor exists solely to be chained from subclass constructors, not to be called directly, which the language already prevents for an abstract class but the access modifier communicates clearly.

An interface is fundamentally different because it cannot hold instance state. Any field you declare in an interface is implicitly `public static final`, which means it is a constant belonging to the interface type itself, not to any instance, and it is initialized when the interface is loaded, not when an object is created. Since there is no per-instance data, there is nothing a constructor could initialize, so the language simply does not permit a constructor in an interface; attempting to write one is a compile error. An interface also cannot be instantiated directly, and even when you write an anonymous class that implements an interface, the constructor that runs is the anonymous class's own constructor plus the implicit `Object` constructor, never an interface constructor.

Several senior-level points round this out. Default and static methods, added in Java 8, gave interfaces behaviour, but they still did not give interfaces instance state, so the no-constructor rule is unchanged. If you genuinely need shared state and shared initialization logic across implementations, that is precisely the signal to use an abstract class rather than an interface, or to combine an interface for the contract with an abstract class for the shared base. The deeper principle is that a constructor's entire job is to initialize instance state during object creation, and because an interface has no instance state and is never the direct type being created, a constructor would have no meaning there.
sections.s3_banking:
At National Bank of India our customers are Rajesh, a software engineer with savings account SAV2001 holding ten lakh rupees, and Priya, a property owner with current account CUR3001 holding two lakh fifty thousand rupees.

Problem 1 — we offer several account types, savings and current, and they all share the same mandatory base data: an account id, a holder name, and a balance, plus the same validation that the id is not blank and the balance is not negative. We kept duplicating this setup and validation in each account type, and one copy drifted and allowed a blank id. We want an abstract base `Account` whose constructor does this shared setup once, so every concrete account type inherits the identical, guaranteed initialization through `super(...)`.

Problem 2 — we also have a contract that any account type must be able to compute its monthly charge, but this contract carries no shared data of its own; it is purely behaviour that each type implements differently. We want to show that this belongs in an interface, and that the interface deliberately has no constructor because it holds no instance state, in contrast to the abstract class which does.

Our runnable demo will define an interface `Chargeable` with a single `monthlyCharge` method and no state, an abstract class `Account` with a protected constructor that initializes and validates the shared fields and provides debit and credit, two concrete subclasses `SavingsAccount` and `CurrentAccount` that call `super(...)` and implement `Chargeable`, and a `main` that creates Rajesh's savings and Priya's current accounts, performs a transfer, and computes each account's monthly charge, logging that the abstract constructor ran for each while the interface contributed only behaviour.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh's savings account (SAV2001, 1000000), Priya's current account (CUR3001, 250000, flat fee 200.00), and a rent amount of 50000.

Step 1 — creating Rajesh's savings account triggers the subclass constructor, whose first statement is `super(...)`. That invokes the abstract `Account` constructor, which validates the id and balance and initializes the shared fields. The log confirms the abstract constructor ran even though `Account` itself can never be instantiated directly.

Step 2 — creating Priya's current account does the same: its `super(...)` runs the identical abstract constructor for the shared setup, and then the subclass sets its own flat fee field. Both accounts received the exact same base initialization through one shared constructor.

Step 3 — the transfer runs. Rajesh is debited 50000 to 950000 and Priya is credited 50000 to 300000, and the success is logged. The debit and credit methods also live in the abstract class, so both account types share that behaviour.

Step 4 — each account's monthly charge is computed through the `Chargeable` interface method. Rajesh's savings balance of 950000 is above the free threshold, so his charge is zero. Priya's current account returns its flat fee of 200.00 because that exceeds the minimum charge constant. The interface contributed only behaviour; it had no constructor and stored no per-instance state, while the shared state came entirely from the abstract class constructor.

Final output:

```text
2026-10-30 19:33:40 INFO    Transfer 50000 from SAV2001 to CUR3001 SUCCESS
2026-10-30 19:33:40 INFO    Rajesh=950000 Priya=300000
2026-10-30 19:33:40 INFO    Rajesh (savings) monthly charge: 0
2026-10-30 19:33:40 INFO    Priya (current) monthly charge: 200.00
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  new SavingsAccount("SAV2001","Rajesh",1000000)
    │ subclass ctor first statement: super(id,name,bal)
    ▼
  abstract Account(id,name,bal)   ← CONSTRUCTOR RUNS (shared setup + validation)
    │ sets accountId, holderName, balance
    ▼ returns to subclass ctor (no extra state for savings)
  fully built SavingsAccount

  new CurrentAccount("CUR3001","Priya",250000,200.00)
    │ super(id,name,bal) → same abstract Account constructor
    ▼ then sets flatFee
  fully built CurrentAccount

  Transfer 50000: Rajesh 1,000,000 → 950,000 ; Priya 250,000 → 300,000

  Chargeable (interface, NO constructor, NO instance state)
    │ monthlyCharge() behaviour only
    ├─ SavingsAccount → balance ≥ 100000 → 0
    └─ CurrentAccount → max(flatFee 200, MIN_CHARGE 50) → 200.00
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Yes, an abstract class can have a constructor, and in practice it usually should. You cannot instantiate an abstract class directly, but it is still a class that can declare instance fields, and those fields need initializing. Its constructor runs as part of building a concrete subclass, invoked through the subclass's super call, and it runs top-down before the subclass body. That makes the abstract class constructor the ideal place to initialize and validate the shared state that every concrete subtype has in common, because the subclass is forced to call super to reach it, so no subtype can ever skip that setup. I often declare it protected to signal that it exists purely to be chained from subclass constructors.

An interface cannot have a constructor, and the reason is fundamental: an interface holds no instance state. Any field you declare in an interface is implicitly public static final, which makes it a constant that belongs to the interface type and is initialized when the interface is loaded, not per object. Since there is no per-instance data and an interface is never the direct type being constructed, there is nothing for a constructor to initialize, so the language does not allow one, and writing a constructor in an interface is a compile error. Even the default and static methods added in Java 8 gave interfaces behaviour but still not instance state, so this rule is unchanged.

The practical guidance I draw from this is that the need for shared state and shared initialization logic is exactly the signal to reach for an abstract class rather than an interface, and often to combine them, using the interface for the contract and the abstract class for the shared base.

In our platform at National Bank of India this is precisely how I structured our account types. We offer savings and current accounts, and they share the same mandatory base data, an id, a holder name, and a balance, along with the same validation that the id is not blank and the balance is not negative. We used to duplicate that setup in each type, and one copy drifted and let a blank id through. I moved it into an abstract Account class with a single protected constructor, so now every concrete account type runs that identical, validated initialization through super, and the drift is impossible. Separately, the requirement that every account can compute its monthly charge carries no shared data of its own, so I expressed it as a Chargeable interface with just the behaviour and a minimum-charge constant. The interface has no constructor because it has no instance state, while the abstract class has one because it owns the shared state, and seeing both side by side is the cleanest way I know to explain why only one of them can have a constructor.
